::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Derivative of Integral with chain rule](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2541164/derivative-of-integral-with-chain-rule), asked by [tooooony](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/492610/tooooony) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-11-28; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> I need to find the derivative (respect to $x$) of the function
>
> $$G(x)=\int _{ { e }^{ x } }^{ sin(x) }{ ln( } { y }^{ 2 })dy$$
>
> By FTC, $A'(x)=ln({ x }^{ 2 })$.
> So far I have
>
> $$G'(x)=\frac { d }{ dx } (A(\sin { x } ))-A({ e }^{ x }))\\ G'(x)=A'(\sin { x } )(\sin { x } )'-A'({ e }^{ x })({ e }^{ x })'\\ G'(x)=ln(\sin ^{ 2 }{ x } )(\cos { x } )-ln({ e }^{ 2x })({ e }^{ x })$$
>
> Can I apply the same method to compute the derivative of  
> $$F(x)=\int _{ sin(x) }^{ cos(x) }{ \frac { 1 }{ \sqrt { 1-{ u }^{ 2 } }  }  } du$$
>
> Any help would be appreciated.
:::

The answer is yes.  It's also worth pointing out that
$$\int_0^y \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\,du = \arcsin y$$
So there ought to be considerable simplification in your derivative.
